cards.register: Common at work and in writing
cards.meaning: A varied mixture of things gathered together for their combined effect or interest.
cards.nuance: The items can be related or completely unrelated. The word often suggests an eclectic collection, and it can also refer to a fragrant blend of dried flowers and spices.

uses.sentence: The final presentation was a potpourri of market trends, customer quotes and competitor examples.
uses.tip: Use it when a collection is deliberately varied rather than focused on one theme.

uses.where: House party · sharing an eclectic playlist
uses.sentence: Her evening playlist was a cheerful potpourri of jazz, folk songs and old film scores.
uses.tip: It adds a slightly literary or sophisticated tone to a description of mixed items.

uses.where: Travel article · describing a market stall
uses.sentence: The stall displayed a potpourri of locally made jewelry, tea and recycled paper goods.
uses.tip: Choose it for a colorful collection; “assortment” is more neutral and businesslike.

origin.summary: Borrowed from French pot-pourri, literally a “rotten pot,” originally referring to a stew made by cooking different ingredients together.

timeline.text: The French term enters English as the name for a mixed meat or vegetable stew.
Its meaning broadens to any mixture or collection of unrelated things.
The word becomes associated with fragrant mixtures of dried flowers, spices and other materials.

cards.pitfall: The stress is normally on the second syllable: pot-POO-ree. The plural is potpourris, and the word can sound overly literary in a brief business message.

cards.meaning: An earlier case, decision or action that can be followed as an example in similar situations.
cards.nuance: Often used when discussing law, business or official decisions. It can mean the example itself or the authority it provides for doing something in the same way.

uses.sentence: The director approved the flexible schedule, which set a precedent for other departments.
uses.tip: Common in the phrase ‘set a precedent’, meaning to create an example others may follow.

uses.sentence: My aunt wore a green dress, so by family precedent, I’m wearing green too.
uses.tip: Here it means an established custom that shapes what people do.

uses.sentence: The ruling could become a precedent for how similar cases are handled.
uses.tip: In legal writing, it usually means a previous decision that influences a later case.

origin.summary: From Latin praecedens, meaning ‘going before’, from praecedere: prae- ‘before’ and cedere ‘to go’.

timeline.text: Praecedere literally means ‘to go before’, and praecedens means ‘going before’.
The word enters English and is used for an example that comes before another case or action.
It refers especially to legal decisions, policies or actions that provide a model for later situations.

cards.pitfall: In legal contexts, ‘precedent’ often has legal force and may constrain later decisions; it is not simply any past event.

cards.meaning: Common or widely found in a particular place, group, or time.
cards.nuance: It describes something that exists broadly rather than being limited to a few cases. Use it when the frequency or reach of a condition, view, or feature is important.

uses.sentence: Delayed deliveries are prevalent across several departments, so we need a shared tracking process.
uses.tip: Use it to describe a problem that affects more than one team or area.

uses.sentence: Cycling to work has become increasingly prevalent in the city.
uses.tip: It sounds informative and neutral, so it works well in everyday conversation.

uses.sentence: The report found that flexible working was prevalent among employees under thirty-five.
uses.tip: Use it when evidence shows that a quality or behaviour is widespread.

origin.summary: From Latin praevalens, meaning ‘prevailing’ or ‘having wider influence’, based on praevalere, ‘to prevail or be widespread’.

timeline.text: Praevalens means ‘prevailing’, ‘predominant’, or ‘in general use’.
The word began appearing in English in medical and general contexts.
It mainly means widespread or common in a particular place or period.

cards.pitfall: Prevalent means widespread, not necessarily dominant; a less common practice can still be prevalent.

cards.meaning: A lack of something essential, especially food, shelter, money or other basic necessities.
cards.nuance: The word is serious and usually describes hardship caused by deprivation. It can also mean simply being without something, but that sense is less common.

uses.sentence: The company’s flexible hours help reduce the privation faced by employees working irregular shifts.
uses.tip: Use it in formal contexts when describing severe lack of basic needs.

uses.sentence: Volunteers are collecting food because winter privation continues to affect many local households.
uses.tip: It sounds more formal and serious than “lack” or “shortage.”

uses.sentence: The report links housing privation to poor health, interrupted education and difficulty finding work.
uses.tip: Often appears in reports and essays about poverty, inequality or social support.

origin.summary: From Latin privatio, meaning “a taking away” or “depriving,” related to privare, “to deprive.” It entered English in the sense of taking away or loss.

timeline.text: Privatio develops from privare, meaning “to deprive” or “take away.”
The word enters English in formal legal and philosophical writing.
It is mainly used for the lack of basic necessities and for severe hardship.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it merely for any inconvenience or minor shortage; it usually suggests a serious lack of necessities.

cards.meaning: The children, grandchildren, and later descendants of a person, family, group, or organism.
cards.nuance: It is a collective noun and can sound formal or literary. It may refer to human descendants or to offspring produced by plants or animals.

uses.sentence: The progeny of the founding family now run several departments across the organisation.
uses.tip: Often used in historical or formal writing about a family’s later generations.

uses.sentence: The progeny of my grandparents ranged in age from nineteen to seventy-two.
uses.tip: A slightly formal alternative to descendants, especially when describing several generations.

uses.sentence: The female produces up to twenty offspring, but few of the progeny survive their first winter.
uses.tip: Common in technical and scientific writing when referring to young organisms collectively.

origin.summary: From Latin progenies, meaning “offspring” or “descendants,” formed from roots meaning “forth” and “to beget.”

timeline.text: Progenies referred to offspring or descendants.
The word began appearing in English in formal and scholarly writing.
It remains mainly formal and is also used in biology.

cards.pitfall: It is usually collective, so avoid saying “one of the progenys”; use “descendant” or “offspring” instead.

cards.meaning: A law or official rule that makes a particular activity or action illegal or forbidden.
cards.nuance: This is a formal word for an enforced ban, often imposed by a government or other authority. It can also refer more broadly to a strong social or moral restriction.

uses.sentence: The new prohibition on sharing customer data applies to every member of the support team.
uses.tip: Use it when describing a strict rule enforced by an organisation or government.

uses.sentence: The prohibition on selling alcohol after ten applies throughout the county.
uses.tip: It sounds more official and specific than simply saying a ban.

uses.where: News report · explaining a new law
uses.sentence: The regulation introduces a clear prohibition on disposable plastic bags in large stores.
uses.tip: Common in legal, political and policy writing when you need a formal term for a ban.

origin.summary: From Latin prohibitio, meaning “a forbidding,” based on prohibere, “to forbid, hold away from, or prevent.”

timeline.text: Prohibere forms from pro-, meaning “before” or “in front of,” and habere, meaning “to hold.”
The Latin-derived word prohibition begins appearing in English legal and religious writing.
It is used for official bans on actions, especially laws or regulations enforced by authorities.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse prohibition, which is a ban or rule, with prohibitionism, which means support for strict bans, especially on alcohol.

cards.meaning: The state of being close or near to someone or something in space, time or relationship.
cards.nuance: Often suggests that closeness brings opportunities, obligations or preferences. It can also refer to the tendency of events or people to come together.

uses.sentence: The law of propinquity often gives preference to relatives who live close to the role.
uses.tip: Usually appears in the phrase “the law of propinquity,” meaning preference for nearby relatives.

uses.sentence: Through daily propinquity, what began as a passing acquaintance developed into a close friendship.
uses.tip: Useful when describing how frequent contact creates closeness.

uses.sentence: The report criticises the design for encouraging propinquity while providing little public space.
uses.tip: A formal alternative to “closeness” or “proximity.”

origin.summary: From Latin propinquitas, meaning nearness or closeness, based on propinquus, meaning near.

timeline.text: Propinquitas means nearness in space, relationship or kinship.
The word enters English, initially with a focus on closeness or proximity.
It is mainly formal, especially in the phrase “the law of propinquity.”

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with propensity, which means a tendency toward a particular behaviour.

cards.meaning: The quality of being suitable, proper or acceptable in a particular situation.
cards.nuance: Often describes behaviour, speech or choices that respect social expectations. It can sound old-fashioned, but it remains common in formal writing.

uses.sentence: There is little propriety in raising a disputed fee before the meal has even begun.
uses.tip: Use it when judging whether an action is appropriate, especially in a professional setting.

uses.sentence: He had the propriety to wait until the speeches ended before mentioning the seating plan.
uses.tip: It can politely suggest that someone crossed a boundary, though it may sound formal.

uses.sentence: I would be grateful if you could consider the propriety of extending the deadline.
uses.tip: A formal alternative to appropriateness when discussing conduct or timing.

origin.summary: From Latin proprietas, meaning ownership or a property, through Old French. Its sense developed from what belongs to someone or is proper for them into what is suitable or socially acceptable.

timeline.text: Proprietas means ownership, a possession or what is proper.
The word enters English through Old French and first refers to ownership or rightful possession.
It develops the sense of suitable or socially acceptable conduct.
It mainly appears in formal discussion of behaviour and social expectations.

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with proprietary, which usually means privately owned or based on intellectual property.

cards.register: Formal; common at work and in institutions
cards.meaning: A set of official rules for how something should be done or how people should behave in a particular setting.
cards.nuance: The word suggests an agreed, orderly process. It is especially common for procedures in organisations, government, diplomacy, research and computing.

uses.sentence: We need a clear protocol for storing passwords and sharing sensitive information.
uses.tip: Use it for a formal procedure that everyone should follow.

uses.sentence: The protocol was to greet each guest before taking our seats at the table.
uses.tip: Here it means the expected rules of polite or ceremonial behaviour.

uses.sentence: The protocol explains how to dispose of the samples safely and record each step.
uses.tip: It fits naturally in documents that lay out a standard method or sequence.

origin.summary: From the ancient Greek protokollon, meaning the first sheet of a document. The word later developed the sense of an official set of rules.

timeline.text: Protokollon referred to the first leaf or cover of a rolled document, from proto, ‘first’, and kollon, ‘leaf’.
Entered English through French and Latin, initially referring to official documents and their formal structure.
Expanded to mean the formal rules observed in diplomacy and ceremonial settings.
Also widely refers to standard procedures in computing, research, healthcare and organisations.

cards.pitfall: In computing, a protocol is a defined method for communication; it is not simply any procedure.

cards.meaning: Clothing or dress, especially formal or ceremonial garments.
cards.nuance: An old-fashioned, literary word with an elevated tone. It usually refers to clothing collectively rather than to one individual garment.

uses.sentence: The curator explained how the embroidered raiment identified the wearer’s rank.
uses.tip: Use it for distinctive or ceremonial clothing in formal historical writing.

uses.sentence: Her flowing raiment transformed an ordinary gown into something from another era.
uses.tip: It sounds poetic or theatrical, so avoid it in casual conversation.

uses.sentence: Despite his fine raiment, the young prince looked nervous before the crowd.
uses.tip: It works well in historical fiction, especially for court dress, robes or ceremonial clothing.

origin.summary: Raiment comes from Middle English raiment, borrowed from Old French raiment, meaning clothing or dress.

timeline.text: Raiment meant clothing, dress or garments.
The word entered Middle English in religious, literary and courtly contexts.
It survives mainly as a formal or literary word, sometimes with a ceremonial tone.

cards.pitfall: Raiment usually means clothing as a whole, so do not use it for one hat, robe or pair of shoes.

cards.meaning: A list of people, often showing who is working, participating or responsible for something.
cards.nuance: A roster often includes duties, dates or contact details. In British English, it can also mean a work schedule.

uses.sentence: The on-call roster is posted every Monday, so check it before your shift.
uses.tip: Common for staff lists, shift schedules and emergency teams.

uses.sentence: I put the barbecue roster on the fridge, but nobody has claimed a dish yet.
uses.tip: In informal English, it can humorously mean a list of guests or jobs.

uses.sentence: Please send the speaker roster by Friday, including each person’s title and email address.
uses.tip: Use it when you need a formal list of people rather than a general description.

origin.summary: The word probably comes through medieval Latin from a term for a list or table, although its exact development is uncertain.

timeline.text: A medieval form of the word was used for a list, roll or table of names.
English adopted it for official lists of soldiers, officials and other participants.
It commonly refers to staff lists, schedules or groups taking part in an event.

cards.pitfall: A roster usually identifies people and may show their roles, but it is not always the same as a rota, which focuses on when duties are performed.

cards.meaning: Connected with the countryside or country life, especially in a simple, natural style.
cards.nuance: It can suggest warm, traditional simplicity, but it may sound mildly disparaging if it implies someone is unsophisticated or awkward.

uses.sentence: The venue has a rustic look, with wooden tables and soft lighting.
uses.tip: Use it for a deliberately simple, countryside-inspired style.

uses.sentence: The guesthouse is rustic, but the beds are comfortable and the breakfast is excellent.
uses.tip: It works when you mean simple and informal rather than luxurious.

uses.sentence: We spent the afternoon walking through a rustic village of stone cottages and narrow lanes.
uses.tip: It paints an atmospheric picture, especially in travel writing.

origin.summary: The word comes through Latin from a root meaning “countryside,” and its early English sense referred to rural life.

timeline.text: Rusticus referred to country life and was formed from rus, meaning “countryside” or “country estate.”
The word entered English with meanings connected to rural places and country customs.
It most often describes a simple, natural or countryside style.

cards.pitfall: Rustic can sound negative when used about people, because it may imply lack of polish or sophistication.

cards.register: Formal in literature; casual at work
cards.meaning: A long, involved story about a family, conflict, or a series of complicated events.
cards.nuance: Today it is often used lightly for an unexpectedly messy or drawn-out process. It can sound dramatic, weary, or humorous rather than strictly literary.

uses.sentence: The software migration became a six-month saga, with three failed launches and endless troubleshooting.
uses.tip: Use it when describing a complicated experience, often with a touch of irony.

uses.sentence: My grandfather’s saga began when he left the village and eventually settled across the coast.
uses.tip: It suggests a sweeping personal story with many episodes and turning points.

uses.where: Novel review · describing a family epic
uses.sentence: Across three generations, the novel becomes a gripping saga of ambition, betrayal, and unexpected love.
uses.tip: Use it for a broad narrative that develops across a long period or many lives.

origin.summary: Saga comes from Old Norse, where it meant a narrative or history. It entered English through Old Norse literature before gaining a modern, broader meaning.

timeline.text: Saga means “a telling, narrative, or history,” especially a story from the past.
The word appears in English through translations and retellings of Icelandic sagas.
It can describe any long, complicated story or ordeal, not only an epic from the past.

cards.pitfall: A saga is usually broad and event-filled; use “story” or “anecdote” for something short and focused.

cards.register: Common in religious contexts; occasional figurative use
cards.meaning: Deliverance from danger, difficulty, or, in religious belief, sin and its consequences.
cards.nuance: It often carries a strong religious meaning, especially when it refers to eternal life. In everyday use, it can dramatically describe a solution that saves someone from a serious problem.

uses.where: Project review · recovering a lost file
uses.sentence: The automatic backup was their salvation when the shared document disappeared.
uses.tip: Use this figuratively for a solution that prevents a serious loss.

uses.where: Family dinner · fixing a travel problem
uses.sentence: Her spare key was the salvation that evening when the others locked themselves out.
uses.tip: The word adds drama or relief, so it suits memorable mishaps.

uses.where: History essay · discussing a religious movement
uses.sentence: The movement promised salvation through faith, forgiveness and a change of life.
uses.tip: In religious writing, check which beliefs the writer is discussing.

origin.summary: The word comes through Old French from Latin, where it was associated with saving someone and being made safe. It developed a major religious meaning through Christian teaching.

timeline.text: Salvationem develops from salvare, ‘to save’, and salus, ‘safety, well-being’.
The word enters English through Old French as salvacion, meaning the act of saving or being saved.
It becomes established for religious deliverance from sin and the promise of eternal life.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use salvation as a simple synonym for saving money or rescuing possessions; the word is more serious and often suggests danger, spiritual need or dramatic relief.

cards.register: Formal; common in legal and public affairs
cards.meaning: A place where someone or something is protected from danger, harm, or disturbance.
cards.nuance: It can mean a physical shelter, legal protection, or a figurative place of peace. It often suggests a stronger sense of safety than refuge.

uses.sentence: The company built a digital sanctuary where employees can disconnect from notifications.
uses.tip: Use it for a protected space where people can focus, recover, or feel safe.

uses.where: Helping a friend · temporary housing crisis
uses.sentence: My friend found temporary sanctuary at our place while she sorted out her housing crisis.
uses.tip: It sounds formal and supportive when describing shelter from danger or serious difficulty.

uses.where: Community report · describing a public space
uses.sentence: The report calls the community garden a sanctuary for residents seeking a quiet break.
uses.tip: Use it in formal writing when a place offers genuine protection, comfort, or relief.

origin.summary: From Latin sanctuarium, meaning a holy place or place of refuge. The Latin word was based on sanctus, meaning holy or protected.

timeline.text: Sanctuarium referred to a sacred place offering protection under Roman law.
The word entered French as sanctuaire, meaning a holy place or refuge.
It entered English for both religious sanctuaries and places of legal protection.
It can describe physical, legal, or figurative protection.

cards.pitfall: Sanctuary suggests real protection or relief, so it may sound excessive for an ordinary favourite chair or quiet corner.

cards.meaning: A serious disagreement that separates a group into different parts.
cards.nuance: It suggests a lasting or organised division, especially within a religion, political party, or organisation. The word often sounds serious and may imply conflict over beliefs or authority.

uses.sentence: The disagreement over the merger created a schism within the leadership team.
uses.tip: Use it when the split affects how a group is organised or managed.

uses.sentence: A schism had formed between the two brothers, and they no longer spoke.
uses.tip: It is stronger than a simple argument and often suggests a lasting separation.

uses.sentence: The schism divided the church for decades and changed how it governed itself.
uses.tip: Common in historical, political, and religious writing.

origin.summary: From Greek skhisma, ‘a separation or split’, which comes from a word meaning ‘to split or tear’. It entered English through Latin in the Middle Ages.

timeline.text: skhisma, ‘separation’ or ‘split’, from skhizein, ‘to split or tear’.
schisma, used for divisions within the early Christian church.
The word appears in English, originally meaning a division in the church.
It describes serious splits within groups, organisations, and political or religious communities.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with a minor disagreement: a schism normally indicates a significant division within one group.

cards.meaning: A descendant of a particular family, especially one from a wealthy, aristocratic or influential family.
cards.nuance: The word can sound admiring when it emphasises a distinguished family line, but it may sound snooty when used about an apparent sense of entitlement.

uses.sentence: She is the scion of a family that has built businesses for three generations.
uses.tip: Use it for a direct descendant, especially when family background is relevant.

uses.sentence: He mentioned that he was a scion of the family whose townhouse now serves as a museum.
uses.tip: It can add a slightly formal or old-fashioned flavour to family talk.

uses.sentence: The scion of an old political family, she entered public life after university.
uses.tip: Often appears at the start of a sentence or after a comma for a formal effect.

origin.summary: The word probably comes through Old French from a Latin word for a descendant or offspring; the exact Latin derivation is uncertain.

timeline.text: The source word meant a descendant or offspring.
The word enters medieval usage in the sense of a descendant.
The word appears in English, initially referring to a descendant.
It usually refers to a descendant of a wealthy, aristocratic or influential family.

cards.pitfall: It means a descendant, not the eldest child, and it is more specific than “heir” unless inheritance is involved.

cards.meaning: A word, phrase, or custom that reveals whether someone belongs to a particular group or shares its loyalties.
cards.nuance: This is a formal, often literary word for a test of belonging or allegiance. It can also refer more broadly to a password, catchphrase, or shared saying.

uses.sentence: Customer trust should be our shibboleth for deciding whether the proposal is genuinely good.
uses.tip: Use it when a shared principle reveals whether someone truly belongs to the team.

uses.sentence: Mentioning an obscure football song was his shibboleth, and everyone knew he supported the club.
uses.tip: It fits when a word or habit marks membership of a close-knit group.

uses.sentence: The phrase became a shibboleth that separated longtime members from newcomers.
uses.tip: It adds a formal tone when describing a phrase that tests allegiance or belonging.

origin.summary: The word comes from the Book of Judges, where opposing people used the pronunciation of a word to identify members of their own group.

timeline.text: People seeking to identify Ephraimites asked them to pronounce a word; those who pronounced it differently were identified as enemies.
The word enters English for a phrase or custom used to test group membership.
It remains a formal word for a test of allegiance, identity, or belonging.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it as a general word for any slogan or motto; it suggests that the words reveal membership or loyalty.

cards.meaning: A particular place where something happens, is built, or can be found, including a place online.
cards.nuance: The word is broad and often points to an official or clearly defined location, such as a construction site, archaeological site, or website.

uses.sentence: All visitors must check in at the site before entering the construction area.
uses.tip: Use it for a place associated with a particular activity or project.

uses.where: Weekend trip · choosing a picnic spot
uses.sentence: We found a quiet site near the river with plenty of shade and room for everyone.
uses.tip: It can sound more formal than “spot” or “place,” especially for a planned or notable location.

uses.sentence: The full report and registration details are available on the event site.
uses.tip: In digital contexts, “site” often means a website or a specific page within one.

origin.summary: The word comes through Old French from Latin situs, meaning “position” or “situation.”

timeline.text: The source word situs referred to a position, place, or situation.
The word entered English through Old French in senses connected with position and location.
It is used for physical locations and, by extension, websites and online destinations.

cards.pitfall: Don't use “site” when you mean a general idea of location; use “place” or “area” instead.

cards.register: Common in serious or professional contexts
cards.meaning: To treat someone or something negatively because of a quality, identity or experience associated with them.
cards.nuance: This word suggests attaching a social label that can damage a person's reputation or sense of belonging. It is stronger and more formal than simply describing someone negatively.

uses.sentence: We should not stigmatize people for taking time off for mental health.
uses.tip: Use it when describing harmful assumptions or discrimination in a workplace.

uses.sentence: Calling teenagers lazy can stigmatize a whole group without recognizing the pressures they face.
uses.tip: It works well when you want to question a label that puts people in a negative category.

uses.sentence: Public campaigns can reduce the stigma surrounding treatment and help people seek support earlier.
uses.tip: Use the noun stigma with surrounding, reduce, tackle or combat to discuss the negative label itself.

origin.summary: From Greek stigma, meaning a mark or stain, especially one associated with disgrace. The word originally referred to a visible mark on someone, then developed into the idea of a social label.

timeline.text: Stigma referred to a mark or stain placed on a person, often as a sign of disgrace.
Reaches English through Latin and French, initially in medical and moral contexts.
Developed into a verb meaning to negatively label or shame someone.

cards.pitfall: Stigmatize means to mark someone negatively; it does not merely mean to describe or identify a characteristic.

cards.meaning: Extremely strict, precise, and demanding, especially about rules or conditions.
cards.nuance: It often suggests that there is very little room for flexibility. It can describe regulations, requirements or demanding tests.

uses.sentence: The security team introduced stringent checks for every request to access customer data.
uses.tip: Use it when rules or controls are unusually strict and exact.

uses.where: Planning an event · discussing entry rules
uses.sentence: There were stringent restrictions on photographs, so we left our phones with the attendant.
uses.tip: It suits formal situations where a rule is being presented as firm and inflexible.

uses.sentence: The report criticizes the project’s stringent deadlines, which left the team with little time for testing.
uses.tip: Often pairs with deadlines, conditions, rules, restrictions or testing.

origin.summary: From Latin stringens, meaning ‘drawn tight’ or ‘strict’, related to stringere, ‘to draw or bind tightly’.

timeline.text: Stringens means ‘drawn tight, strict, or exacting’.
The word enters English with the sense of being tight or strict.
It mainly describes rules, requirements, tests and conditions that allow little freedom.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with stringant, which means conspicuous or obvious in American English.

cards.meaning: The right to vote in political elections.
cards.nuance: Most often used in political, historical and legal contexts. It can also refer more broadly to voting or the act of casting a vote.

uses.sentence: The campaign wants to protect voting access and make suffrage easier for rural communities.
uses.tip: Use it when discussing voting rights or access to elections.

uses.sentence: The exhibition shows how women organised for suffrage before receiving the vote in Britain.
uses.tip: In this context, it usually refers to the campaign for women’s voting rights.

uses.sentence: The reform expanded suffrage by removing property restrictions from the electoral system.
uses.tip: Pairs naturally with universal, limited, equal and parliamentary.

origin.summary: From Anglo-French suffrage, meaning ‘a vote’, which came from Latin suffragium, a word associated with voting and support.

timeline.text: Suffragium referred to a vote, decision or expression of support.
The word entered English through Anglo-French in the sense of a vote.
It became closely associated with campaigns for women’s right to vote.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse suffrage with suffragette or suffragist: those describe women or activists involved in the British campaign for women’s voting rights.

cards.meaning: A belief or practice based on luck, fear, or ideas that cannot be supported by evidence or reasoning.
cards.nuance: Often describes an old ritual, sign, or saying that people follow even though it has no proven connection to the result they expect.

uses.sentence: The team treats the old rule about opening presentations on Friday as a superstition.
uses.tip: Useful when gently separating a team tradition from evidence-based practice.

uses.sentence: My grandmother refuses to walk under a ladder, although she knows it is only a superstition.
uses.tip: Often appears in conversations about luck, customs, and family beliefs.

uses.sentence: The report describes the ceremony as a superstition rather than evidence that the ritual prevents misfortune.
uses.tip: Pairs well with words such as belief, ritual, fear, and folklore.

origin.summary: From Latin superstitio, meaning excessive fear or awe, and later an unreasonable belief. English borrowed it through medieval Latin and French.

timeline.text: Superstitio originally referred to excessive fear, awe, or anxiety about religious signs.
The word entered English with meanings connected to unreasoned fear and religious practice.
It mainly means a belief or ritual based on luck rather than evidence.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it for every old belief or custom; it implies that the belief lacks a rational or evidential basis.

cards.meaning: The practical application of scientific knowledge, tools and methods to solve problems or make tasks easier.
cards.nuance: The word can refer to a particular invention or tool, or to a wider field of innovation. It often sounds positive when discussing progress, but can also prompt concern about jobs, privacy or unequal access.

uses.sentence: New technology has reduced the time we spend preparing monthly reports.
uses.tip: Common when discussing tools, systems and ways of working.

uses.sentence: I’m trying to use technology less at bedtime so I can sleep better.
uses.tip: Useful when talking about technology’s impact on everyday life.

uses.sentence: Investment in technology will support remote work and improve customer service.
uses.tip: Pairs naturally with investment, development, advances and innovation.

origin.summary: Built from Greek roots meaning ‘craft’ or ‘skill’ and ‘study’, originally referring to the systematic study of the practical arts.

timeline.text: The roots techne, meaning ‘craft or skill’, and logia, meaning ‘study’, form the basis.
Technology enters English with the sense of the systematic study or description of the practical arts.
The meaning expands to include the tools and methods used to apply scientific knowledge.
It commonly refers both to technology as a field and to specific devices, systems and techniques.

cards.pitfall: Technology is not exactly the same as technique: technology often implies tools or applied science, while technique can be any method or skill.

cards.meaning: Thespian means theatrical or exaggeratedly dramatic, and as a noun it means an actor, especially one associated with classical or Shakespearean theatre.
cards.nuance: When used as an adjective, it can suggest that someone is performing rather than speaking naturally. As a noun, it has a slightly old-fashioned or literary tone.

uses.sentence: His thespian outburst made everyone uncomfortable, so we moved on to the actual problem.
uses.tip: Use it when behaviour is noticeably theatrical, melodramatic or performed for attention.

uses.sentence: Her thespian retelling of the traffic accident had us all in stitches.
uses.tip: It can describe an exaggerated performance without being completely hostile.

uses.sentence: The play delivered its thespian energy through bold staging and oversized performances.
uses.tip: The word is useful in reviews when you want to praise or describe overt theatricality.

origin.summary: From the name Thespis, an ancient Greek poet traditionally regarded as the founder of theatre. The word came to mean an actor and later broadened to describe theatrical behaviour.

timeline.text: Thespis, a poet from the sixth century BCE, is traditionally linked with the beginning of theatre.
The spelling thespian appears in English in connection with actors and theatre.
It means an actor or, as an adjective, theatrical and sometimes exaggerated.

cards.pitfall: In modern use, thespian often implies exaggerated or affected behaviour, not simply any actor.
